en: The Mahāpadma Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperial Censor and Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
Great Master of Enlightened Teaching, Subject Faxian, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Venerable Elder Kāśyapa was wandering through the country of Kośala and, proceeding by stages, arrived at the northern part of the great city of Śrīṣa, where he stayed in the Deer Park of the Śrīṣa Forest.
At that time, there was a king named Mahāsaṃmata who resided in the city of Śrīṣa.
This king had previously lacked faith in the law of cause and effect, and he would often say:
"There is no future world, there are no persons, and furthermore, there is no rebirth by transformation."
They constantly gave rise to such nihilistic views (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
At that time, in the great city of Śirīṣa, there were great brahmins, elders, and leaders who said to one another:
"How is it that this young śramaṇa Kāśyapa has come to this city, to the Deer Park in the Śirīṣa Forest to the north?"

At that time, the Venerable Kāśyapa’s fame was widely renowned throughout that city. All the people of the city had long heard that Kāśyapa was skilled in expounding the essential points of the Dharma and constantly taught various profound and subtle meanings; that he had attained freedom from illness and always practiced the dhūta ascetic virtues, and that he was indeed a worthy recipient of offerings and a great arhat.
"Now that he has come here, we should all go together to that grove to pay our respects, visit him, and make offerings.

Thereupon, the great brahmins and elders of the city all departed from the north of the city and proceeded to the Śirīṣa Grove in the Deer Park, desiring to pay their respects and inquire after his well-being.

At that time, King Mahā-samyakpada, from atop his high tower, saw from afar the brahmins, elders, and others within the city all departing together; they were traveling toward the north of the city to go to the Śirīṣa Forest in the Deer Park.
Having seen this, the king asked his attendants:
"Why have the brahmins and elders of the city all gone out together to the Śirīṣa Forest in the Deer Park?"
The attendant ministers addressed the King, saying:

"There is a śramaṇa named Kāśyapa the Younger who, while traveling for the sake of conversion, has arrived here and is currently residing in the Deer Park at the Śirīṣa Forest to the north of this great city."
"Therefore, let all the brahmins and householders within the city go forth together from the city to pay their respects, visit, and make offerings.
Upon hearing this report, the King immediately said to his attendant ministers:

"You should go there and announce to that assembly of brahmins and householders: 'You should stop for a moment and wait briefly; I shall arrive soon and go there with you all to pay our respects and visit the śramaṇa, the youth Kāśyapa.'"

Why is this? It is because it is my fear that you brahmins and elders may have been led astray by the false teachings of that young śramaṇa Kāśyapa; thus, without relying on true knowledge, you falsely claim that there is a self, that there is a future world, and that there is rebirth through transformation.
Then, having received the king’s command, that attendant went to the place where the brahmins and householders were and proclaimed the royal decree to the assembly, saying:
"The Great King Ṛtuparṇa proclaims:
'Cease for a moment; I shall soon arrive and go with you to pay homage to the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa.'"
The assembly of people, having received the command, did not dare to move forward.
At that time, the attendant minister, having delivered the king’s decree, returned to the king’s presence and reported:

“Your servant has just received the command to go to the assembly of brahmins and householders and convey the holy will in its entirety, instructing the brahmins and householders to wait for a moment, as the King will arrive shortly to pay his respects together with you all to the śramaṇa youth Kāśyapa.”
Having received these orders, that multitude ceased and did not proceed.
Then King Śaddanta, having prepared his chariot and retinue, departed from the palace city and went together with the assembly of brahmins and householders to the Deer Park at the Śirīṣa Forest.

The king’s mind was filled with pride; when his carriage reached a place where it could no longer pass, he finally descended and proceeded on foot until he arrived at the Venerable One’s dwelling within the garden.

At that time, King Samyak-vākya, together with the assembly of brahmins and householders, had not yet placed faith in or held the Venerable Kumāra-Kāśyapa in high esteem, nor did they treat him with great reverence.

The King and the Venerable One exchanged greetings with one another, after which the King withdrew to sit at one side; at that time, the assembly of brahmins and elders, seeing the King act in such a manner, also behaved with a degree of gravity, and all together surrounded him and remained there.
At that time, the Great King addressed him with these words:
"Venerable Kāśyapa,
please listen to my words."
"As it appears to my mind, there is no future world, nor are there any persons, nor is there any rebirth by transformation.
Such is my view; what do you think, Venerable One?
Kāśyapa replied:
“If Your Majesty would wish to hear such righteous principles, you should first abide in sincere faith.
The King then replied,
“Indeed, I shall receive your instruction.”
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the Great King, saying:
"Does Your Majesty perceive the sun and moon as existing or non-existing?
This world and the world beyond are evident in principle; without troubling Your Majesty, how should one see them, and how should one hear of them?"
The King said,
“Kāśyapa! As for these suns and moons, both in this world and in future worlds, my own observations and learning are identical to those of the Venerable One.”
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"As Your Majesty perceives it, the sun and moon exist; so it shall be in the future world as well, Great King!"
"You should not cling to it as you previously saw it.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Great King!..."

One should know that for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, up to those who are Worthy of Offerings and World-Knowers, there must certainly exist causes and effects pertaining to this world and the next; they have personally realized this through wisdom and understood it as it truly is.
"Great King!
You should not persist in the view of annihilationism as you did before.
At that time, the Great King remained deluded and unreflective; he said to Kāśyapa:
"Why do you now speak such words?
As I understand it, there truly is no future world; therefore, Kāśyapa, do not persist in speaking thus.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa replied to the Great King:
"Is this very body of the King presently existent or non-existent?
If you consider this body of the King to be existent, how can you hold the view of annihilationism and claim there is no future life?
By what analogy should this principle be proven?"
The Great King replied:
"Venerable Kāśyapa!
I now have a parable to illustrate this principle: the present body exists, but the future life is non-existent."
The king said: “Kāśyapa!
Suppose a member of my own family falls ill, and after suffering for a long time, is on the verge of death; I would then go to them to inquire after their condition and say:”
"Your illness is grave and deep; I know for certain that it cannot be overcome. Should you pass away, I have something most earnest to entrust to you.
I had previously heard this from śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas:
"If a person breaks the precepts and commits evil deeds, after the end of life they will fall into hell."
"If what these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas say is true, then after you relatives have passed away, you will certainly fall into hell. Why is this?"
Your kinsmen have broken the precepts and committed transgressions; by this you should know that they will certainly fall into the evil realms.
If they are in the evil realms, they shall either dispatch a messenger or come themselves to inform me:
"We are now in hell, undergoing extreme suffering."
"If you were to come and inform me, I would certainly go to rescue you;
yet there has only ever been one who went, and never one who returned.
Kāśyapa!"
"In my opinion, using this as an analogy, there is certainly no future life.
Kāśyapa replied, "Great King!"
Although this analogy has been presented, it does not constitute a correct explanation.
I now ask the King: suppose there were a person who violated the king’s law and was seized by the patrol guards;
they would be brought before the King and say to him, "This man has committed such a crime, and I dare not conceal it."

Upon hearing this report, the King immediately issued an edict to the relevant officials, ordering that the culprit be bound hand and foot with his body secured firmly, and driven to a crossroads where many people gather, with drums beaten to announce:
"This criminal has now violated such-and-such a law."
"Thus it was proclaimed throughout the city, in the east, west, south, and north, so that all might hear and know. Subsequently, he was led out of the city to be executed according to the law.

The officials, obeying the command, immediately bound the hands of the culprit behind his back and secured his body firmly; they were then driven to a crossroads where many people gathered, and a drum was beaten to announce:
'This criminal has violated such a law.'"

"Throughout the city—in the east, west, south, and north—proclamations were issued everywhere in accordance with the King’s decree. Once the officials and commoners learned of this, they drove him out of the city and executed him according to the law."
When such a sinner approaches the time for his execution, he says to the guardians:
"I pray that you will show me compassion and release me for a short while, so that I may go briefly to my home to bid farewell to my relatives."
"Great King!
Would that prison guard dare to release him for even a moment to let him return home?
The King said:
"No, Kāśyapa! Even if this person were to lament most piteously and earnestly, that jailer would still not dare to release him."
"Why is this? According to the laws of the kingdom, there can be no temporary pardon.
Venerable Kāśyapa spoke again:
“Great King!
Because of their sinful karma, the King’s kinsmen, after the end of their lives, have fallen into hell, where they constantly undergo bitter suffering due to that sinful karma.”
These sinners addressed the wardens of hell, begging for temporary release to return to the human world, so that they might go before the King and seek his deliverance from suffering.
"Great King! they cried.
"Would these hell-wardens ever be willing to release him?
The King replied, "No."
Kāśyapa spoke again: “Great King!
The principle is the same as that which exists in the world: there is no logic for even a moment’s release.”
"Great King!
Do not equate this analogy with the world to come; to hold such a view is the adherence to nihilism and is not the correct principle.

Therefore, you should know that just as there is this present life, there is certainly a future life. Even for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, arhats, and world-knowers who have realized the truth through their own wisdom, they should no longer maintain such views as those previously held."
The king replied again:
"Venerable Kāśyapa!
These words do not accord with my intention and are not yet acceptable; you should not further claim that there truly is a future world."
Furthermore, Kāśyapa replied to the Great King:
"If this is your intention, O King, is there no further analogy that might serve as proof?
The King said:
“Kāśyapa! I now have yet another analogy concerning kinsmen that can serve as proof.
Kāśyapa!”
Suppose my own relatives were afflicted by a grave illness; as their lives were about to end, I would entrust them to you and say to the patient:
"I have heard that śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas often say this:

'If a person maintains the precepts and cultivates various wholesome dharmas, or practices giving with the three spheres purified, and does not give rise to envy upon seeing others' excellence, such a person will, at the end of life, be reborn in the heavenly realms.'"
"If what those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas have said is true, then at the end of your life you will surely be reborn in the heavenly realms.

Why is this? I observe that you have always maintained the precepts and cultivated wholesome dharmas; you practice giving with the three spheres purified, and you harbor no envy toward the excellence of others. By this, you may know for certain that you will be reborn in the heavenly realms."
"If you succeed in being reborn in heaven, you should send a messenger, or perhaps come yourself, to inform me:
'I have now been reborn in such-and-such a heaven and am experiencing happiness.'"
“Kāśyapa! If my kinsmen had truly been reborn in heaven, they would surely have come to inform me. Why is it that my kinsmen, having merely witnessed my death, have not come to report it?”
"By this you should know that there is certainly no future life.
Kāśyapa said to the Great King:
"I now wish to speak another parable once more, so that Your Majesty may see that a future life truly exists."
"Great King!
It is like a foul pit, so stinking that one cannot approach it. Suppose a person were to accidentally fall into it; finding the stench and filth unbearable, he employs skillful means to escape.

Once his body has emerged, he bathes in water boiled with various perfumes and further anoints his body with fragrant unguents. His body being now pure and fragrant, he adorns himself with exquisite Kāśika garments and precious flower garlands, remaining at home and enjoying happiness."
"Great King!
What do you think?
Would such a person ever again take pleasure in entering that former foul pit?"
The king said, "No, Kāśyapa!"
"That foul and loathsome pit is not a place where people find delight.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Great King!"
The birth of that person in heaven is likewise so; once born in heaven, how could they ever again think of returning to the human realm?
"Furthermore, Great King!
"A hundred years for humans is but a single day and night for the Trāyastriṃśa gods.

Great King, your kinsmen have practiced various wholesome dharmas; having been born in the celestial realm, they enjoy pleasure day and night. How could they possibly think further of returning to repay you, [saying], 'I am born in the celestial realm and enjoy pleasure day and night'?"
"Great King!
Is the length of your lifespan equal to that of devas?
The king replied:
"No, Kāśyapa," he replied. Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Great King!

The celestial realm and the human realm are fundamentally separated; one should not expect a reciprocal response from them like a fool might hope for, and only then can one believe in the existence of future lives."
"Great King!

Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who are worthy of offerings and understanders of the world—even unto those who must know that there is a future life—should realize it as it truly is through their own wisdom; they should not further maintain the view that there is no future life."
The King replied to Kāśyapa:
“Even what the Venerable One says cannot yet be trusted. Why is this?”

Regarding what was said—that one hundred years among humans is equivalent to one day and night in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—who came to inform you that one hundred years among humans is equivalent to one day and night in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven?
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“The analogy you have seen, O King, is like that of one born blind. Why is this so?”
A person born blind, who from the very beginning has never seen the colors blue, yellow, red, or white, nor the characteristics of form—whether subtle or coarse, long or short—might then say:
"From the beginning, there have been no such colors as blue, yellow, red, or white, nor any characteristics of form, whether subtle or coarse, long or short."
He further said:
"I do not know it, nor do I see it.

Because this person born blind could not see for himself, he then insisted that such color-and-form characteristics as blue, yellow, red, white, or even long and short had never existed from the beginning.
"Great King!
Do not be like one born blind who clings to the notion that there are no forms.
The King said:
“Kāśyapa! According to my own understanding, if that heavenly realm truly existed, I would say it exists; since it fundamentally does not exist, how could I say that it truly exists?”
He spoke again:
"Kāśyapa! You are no virtuous man."
Why is this? I see my own original correctness; how then can you compare me to one who is born blind? Kāśyapa!

As for the matters you previously mentioned, such as being reborn in heaven and so forth, I truly do not believe them; were I to believe such words, it would be like consuming poisonous medicine, like a blade falling upon one's body, or like climbing a mountain only to fall and bring about one's own death.
"In this way, I shall avoid all such evils.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa replied to the Great King:
"I recall that in the past there was a brāhmaṇa who was immensely wealthy and advanced in years. He had an only son, barely sixteen years of age, whose mother passed away."
That brahmin, unable to remain a widower, eventually married again; not long after, his wife became pregnant, and before she had given birth, the brahmin also passed away.
Thereupon, the son said to his stepmother:
"All the household wealth, gold, silver, precious jewels, and even all articles of enjoyment belong entirely to me; there is no one else who shares in my property."
When the stepmother heard her son’s words, she immediately said to him:
"The body of your father that I now carry within me shall be raised until it is grown, and then it shall be divided equally with you."
The son spoke of the matter once more at that time, whereupon his mother thought to herself:
"This child is young and of a foolish and ignorant disposition; though I have spoken with him in depth, he has not yet understood."

Furthermore, out of greed and attachment, desiring to deliver the child quickly, she employed many expedient means to seek a speedy birth; though the months were not yet full, she instead damaged the fetus.
Great King!
"Because of greed and jealousy, that woman instead harmed her own pregnancy; Great King!
Now, because of ignorance, you have given rise to the view of annihilationism.
The King replied again:
“Venerable Kāśyapa!
Do not speak as you did before.

By upholding the precepts, cultivating goodness, and practicing generosity, one will be reborn in the heavens after the end of this life, where one’s lifespan is long and one dwells eternally in happiness.”
I truly do not believe it.
If I were now to believe the words of Kāśyapa, it would be like consuming poison, receiving a sword and blade, or falling from a high mountain to take my own life.
"How is it, Kāśyapa,
that you speak so firmly?
According to my own view, there certainly is no person, nor is there a future world, nor is there rebirth by transformation."
Furthermore, Kāśyapa said to the Great King:
"Is there no further analogy to illustrate this matter?
The King replied:
“Kāśyapa, I shall provide another parable to demonstrate this matter, so that you may know that there is no person, no future world, and no beings of miraculous birth. Kāśyapa!”

If any of my relatives were to fall gravely ill, I would immediately go to them to offer comfort and inquire after their welfare; as long as their lives had not yet ended, they would still speak with me about their suffering, but once their lives had come to an end, there would be no one left to tell me of their distress.
"By this it may be known that there is certainly no future life, nor is there any rebirth by transformation.
Kāśyapa replied:
"I recall that in the past there was a village where the people did not know the characteristics of a conch, nor had they ever heard the sound of one."

Suddenly, a man came from outside and arrived at that village, where he stayed. This man constantly took up a conch shell as his primary task; every day he would take the shell, go before the sacred image, blow it as an offering, and once the offering was complete, return to his dwelling place.
At that time, all the people in the village suddenly heard the sound of the conch and were all struck with wonder and alarm;
they said to one another, "What is this sound?
It is something none of us have ever heard before."
"O Great King!
At that time, all the people of the village went together to the place where the conch was, and asked the conch:
'From where have you come? Answer us truthfully; if you do not speak the truth, we shall break you. Knowing my intention, the conch quickly explained its origin."
"O Great King!

Those people had never before seen or heard of that conch-shell mark or the sound of the conch. They wished to have the conch engage in dialogue with them; yet since the conch is insentient, how could it possibly speak in reply?"
Why is this? It is just as if, Great King, one were to wish to engage in conversation with a person whose life has ended; since that person’s life is exhausted, how could they possibly speak again?
"Great King, you should not hold such a view, namely that there is no person, no future world, and no beings born by transformation.
Kāśyapa spoke again:

"There are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess the divine eye; with their purified divine eye, they see clearly how persons die here and are reborn there, receiving bodies that are good or evil, handsome or ugly, and whether they are born in the heavens or fall into the miserable realms."
"Great King!
Such matters as these can all serve as proof; you should no longer say that there is no future world nor rebirth by transformation.
The King said:
“Kāśyapa! Although you have offered this analogy, it does not satisfy my mind.
According to my view, there certainly is no person, nor is there any birth by transformation, nor is there a future world.”
Furthermore, Kāśyapa said to the Great King:
"If this is so, what further analogy can be used to prove that there is no person, no future world, and no spontaneous birth?"
The King said:
"Venerable Sir!

It is like an official who enforces the law and governs the people, yet when he himself presides over affairs, he violates the regulations. Later, having been impeached, the King becomes fully aware of it and issues an edict to the judicial authorities to adjudicate the offender according to the law."
The king commanded again:

"Bind the hands of that criminal and lead him to the place of execution to be punished with severity; bind him with ropes and weigh him on a scale, then flay his skin and pare his flesh, suspending him in another location."
This person, while still alive, is aware of their suffering; once life has been severed, there is no longer any sound or breath.

Furthermore, at the moment that sinner’s life is about to end, the body becomes supple, but once life has been severed, the body becomes rigid and stiff; thus, there are differences regarding lightness or heaviness, and life or death.
"Venerable One!
By this I know that there is certainly no future life, nor is there anyone who is reborn, nor is there any spontaneous birth.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“Great King!
What do you think?
For example, iron balls also differ in being light or heavy, soft or hard; when the iron is hot, its substance is light and soft, but after the iron has cooled, it becomes heavy and hard.”
"Great King!

Sentient and insentient beings alike receive the four great elements; because those four great elements undergo combination and dispersal, there arise distinctions such as softness and hardness, cold and heat. Do not apply this principle to the afterlife or to beings of miraculous birth."

"Great King, you should know that there truly exist those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess the divine eye; they see beings dying here and being born there, even down to their beauty or ugliness, and whether they are reborn in the heavens or fall into the evil destinies—all of which can be verified. Thus, the existence of future lives and of spontaneous birth (upapāduka) is indeed real."
The King said:
"Venerable One!
What you have said is not yet trustworthy."
"In my view, there truly is no person, no future world, and no rebirth by transformation.

under Imperial Decree. Furthermore, Kāśyapa addressed the Great King, saying:
"Is there no further analogy that could prove that there is no person, no future world, and no rebirth by transformation?
The King replied,
"I have another analogy that can prove this principle."
"Venerable One!
It is just as if there were a person who had committed an extremely grave crime, and a close minister, having learned of it, immediately informed the king:
'There is now this person who has committed an extremely grave crime.'"
Once the king had learned this, he ordered the relevant authorities to seize and bind the culprit and adjudicate the case according to the law.
The judicial officials, having received the command, immediately took the culprit, bound his two hands, and boiled him in a cauldron.
He further issued a command, saying:

"Once their flesh has rotted away and their bones are clearly visible, you may stir them within the cauldron with a staff and search minutely for those from future generations or those born by transformation who enter and exit."

The legal officials, obeying the command, followed the King’s instructions exactly; when the contents had reached the state of being thoroughly decomposed, they stirred the cauldron and searched for anyone who might have entered or exited from the afterlife, such as those born by transformation, yet they saw none at all. Even as they searched repeatedly and in successive layers, they still saw nothing.
The king said,
"Venerable sir!
By this analogy, one knows that in reality there is no person, no future world, and no beings of miraculous birth."
Thereupon Kāśyapa addressed the Great King, saying: "Great King!

It is like a person who, while asleep, dreams of a magnificent garden. Within that garden are various kinds of trees, with flowers and fruits in full bloom and ponds of pristine clarity; in his dream, the person finds it exceedingly delightful."
"Great King!
Does that grove truly exist?
Furthermore, as for looking upon it, enjoying it, and entering or leaving it—is that real?"
The king said, "No, Kāśyapa!"
"Whatever is seen in a dream is not real.
Kāśyapa replied, "It is just like the view of annihilationism held by Your Majesty; it is not real."
"Great King!

One must truly and sincerely know that there are beings, that there is a future world, and that there is rebirth by transformation; even that there are truly śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess the pure divine eye that transcends the world, and who see beings dying here and being born there—whether handsome or ugly, or those who attain birth in heaven or fall into hell."
"This is the truth; you should no longer cling to the view of annihilationism as you did before.
The King said, "Venerable One!"
"Why do you repeatedly speak in this manner?
According to my own understanding, I know for certain that there is no self (pudgala), no future world, and no rebirth by transformation.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa replied to the Great King:
"Furthermore, what analogy can be used to prove that there is no person, no future world, and no rebirth by transformation?
The King said,
"Venerable One!"
I shall further provide an analogy to substantiate this principle.

Suppose there is a person who, while carrying out royal affairs, violates the established regulations; a close minister reports this to the King, who then becomes fully aware of it and orders the case to be handed over to the legal authorities for interrogation to ascertain the facts.

Since their offenses were grave, he ordered them to be subjected to severe punishment: first having their skin and flesh cut away, then severing their tendons and veins, breaking their bones and extracting their marrow, all in search of those born from humans or those born by transformation.

The judge, having received his orders, applied the law as prescribed; not daring to transgress what the King had said, he searched sequentially within the skin, flesh, sinews, veins, marrow, and bones for humans and beings of miraculous birth, yet from beginning to end, he saw neither humans nor beings of miraculous birth.
"Venerable One!
By this analogy, one knows that in reality there is no person, nor is there any spontaneous birth, nor is there a future world.
Kāśyapa replied:
"Great King!
I recall that in the past, there was a practitioner who dwelt in the mountains.
At that time, a merchant caravan, having loaded many wagons with goods, stopped near the practitioner’s hut for the night before departing."

Then, at dawn, that practitioner went to inspect his lodging for fear of having left any belongings behind; indeed, he found there a young boy who had only recently been weaned and was unable to distinguish east from west, whom the merchants had left behind by oversight.
The practitioner of the Way, out of compassion and pity, feared that the boy might be harmed by hunger and thirst; he took him back to his hermitage and nurtured him like a close relative.

This practitioner’s practice was centered on the worship of fire; he constantly focused his mind on maintaining the fuel, adding wood to the flames so they were never extinguished. As the years passed and months went by, the boy gradually grew up until he was fifteen or sixteen years old.
The practitioner thought to himself,
"The youth has grown up and is now capable of being entrusted with responsibilities.
One day, as the practitioner had business that required him to enter the city, he left the hermitage for a short time and instructed the youth:
"I have some business that requires me to go out for a short while. As for the fire in the hut, you must add wood to it every day as I do, and ensure it does not go out.
Having said this, he departed.

Once the practitioner had departed, the boy remained foolish and ignorant, still preoccupied with his play; because of his attachment to play, he forgot about the fire, and as no fuel was added, the fire was eventually extinguished.
At that time, having seen the fire extinguished, the youth gathered the firewood and piled it within the hearth, speaking these words of incantation:
"O Fire, come forth quickly! If you do not come forth, I shall destroy you."
"Thus, although that boy entreated him with bitter urgency, the fire would not come out at all.
Because the fire did not come out, he spoke even more harsh words:
'If the fire does not come out, I shall also beat you.'"
At that time, the youth sought fire but could not produce it; his heart was immediately filled with anxiety and fear, thinking:
"When the practitioner returns, he will surely disgrace me.
He stood to one side, contemplating the matter of the fire.
When the practitioner had finished his duties and returned to the hermitage, he saw the boy sitting in silence and knew at once that the fire had gone out.
He said to the boy, "Did you become greedy for negligence and cause the fire to go out?"
The youth replied:
"I momentarily forgot, and the fire has already gone out.
After the fire was extinguished, I piled firewood in the hearth and prayed with both good and evil words that the fire would not emerge."
The practitioner said:
"You are truly foolish!
If the fire has already been extinguished, you must obtain fire before it can burn again."

I have never heard of fire spontaneously emerging from a pile of firewood placed upon cold ashes; even if you were to pile immeasurable wood in your furnace and employ many expedients, you would only exhaust yourself in vain, for there would be no way to obtain fire.
"O Great King!

This youth seeking fire within the ashes after the fire has been extinguished is just like Your Majesty, who is deluded and will not turn back from error; he searches for a human being or a spontaneously born being within a corpse, falsely clinging to the notion that no person exists and thus giving rise to the view of nihilism."
"Great King!
You ought to know that there truly are persons, there is birth by transformation, and there is a future world.
The King said:
“Venerable sir!
Do not speak thus.
If I were to follow you and say that there is a future world, I would surely be the subject of public criticism.”
Why is this? For now the people of this capital are saying:
"Since ancient times, the King has not believed in cause and effect; he has constantly said that there is no future world, nor are there any persons, nor is there any spontaneous birth."
"Today, however, I have followed the transformation brought about by Kāśyapa.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Great King!"

I recall that in the past there were two merchant leaders, both of whom possessed such wealth and treasures that none in their country surpassed them. Later, at one time, they made an agreement to become companions and traveled together to another land to trade goods and seek profit.

These two merchant leaders each gathered their respective merchants as companions; they then loaded many carts and yoked horses and mules, setting out on the road together that very day to travel toward their destination.

Having already traveled far from their country, with hardships and perils close at hand, a caravan leader who was already familiar with the fact that there were dangers ahead on this road said to another caravan leader:
"Do you know this now?"
"The path ahead is perilous and devoid of human habitation; since the caravan is large, it is prudent to prepare in advance.

After the two leaders had deliberated thus, one leader set out first, intending that with fewer people his needs would be easily met. He took along all provisions of rice, flour, and food, as well as firewood.

In the midst of his journey, he suddenly encountered a man coming to meet him; the man was large and black of body with both eyes blood-red, his hair on the crown was thin and sparse, and his clothing was tattered and ragged. He drove a donkey-cart that appeared like a ghost.
The merchant leader asked:
"Venerable sir!
Will there be food, drink, firewood, and other such provisions along the road ahead?"
The man replied:

"On the road ahead there is an abundance of food, drink, firewood, and other provisions; none shall be lacking. You may discard everything you are carrying so that you are not hindered by the weight as you proceed."
At that time, having heard these words, the merchant leader said to the caravan:

"You members of the assembly have all heard what was said; since food, drink, and other necessities will not be lacking along the road ahead, why carry extra items beyond our needs to exhaust our carts and horses?"
The merchant leader and his companions were all unwise men; they simply cast away what they carried and departed.

On the first day of their journey, by the time the sun set, there was nothing but a vast wilderness where no signs of human habitation were encountered. Looking in all directions, it was desolate and nothing could be found for sustenance. Lacking food and drink, they all suffered from hunger and thirst; enduring this misery throughout the night, they pressed on with great effort. On the second day, they again traveled until nightfall, remaining in the wilderness with nothing else to behold.
The merchants deliberated together regarding what they had previously encountered; reflecting upon his appearance, they were certain that he was a ghost:
"We were ignorant and blindly believed his words; this wicked deceiver has deluded us to such an extent."
On the third day, both men and horses were utterly exhausted and unable to proceed further; looking at one another in silence, they remained there awaiting death.
That merchant leader, traveling on the following day, also encountered these same people coming to meet him, who asked:
"Is there any food, drink, or other necessary provisions along the road ahead?"
That person, as before, spoke falsely one by one:
"Our requirements for food and drink are not lacking at all; what use have we for these heavy and cumbersome wagons and horses?
You should know that these things may be discarded."

Later, there was a merchant leader who was wise and intelligent; whatever he undertook, he would first deliberate. He already knew that this road contained vast wildernesses and perilous places, and having measured the distance, he realized the difficulties were not far off. Furthermore, observing that this man’s countenance was unusual and his belongings coarse and shabby, he feared he might be a deceptive impostor and not to be trusted; thus, he consulted with the other merchants before proceeding.

On the third day, he suddenly encountered the aforementioned caravan leader and his merchants by the roadside, who were standing there exhausted from hunger. When he inquired as to their situation, he learned that they too had been misled by the encounter with that hideous person and the deceptive demoness.

The merchants deliberated together and immediately shared their respective portions of food and drink, distributing them equally to one another so that all the merchants might together cross over the perilous terrain.
Great King!
That merchant leader, out of ignorance, believed those deceptive and false words and was brought to great suffering on a perilous road.
Great King!
Because of ignorance, you have grasped at the view of annihilationism; you will surely undergo great suffering for a long night.
At that time, having heard these words, the Great King said to the Venerable One:
"Do not offer further analogies; my mind shall not turn back. Why is this?

"I fear that the people of that country will say of me that I lack steadfastness, for King Prasenajit has always declared: 'In truth, there is no person, nor is there birth by transformation, nor is there a future world,' yet today he has been converted by Kāśyapa."
"Therefore, I do not now alter my former view.
At that time, Kāśyapa again addressed the king, saying:
"In the past, there were two men who possessed meager wealth. They formed a partnership to conduct business; although their capital was different, they shared in the profits."
Having finalized their agreement, they chose an auspicious day to set out, and before many days had passed, they reached another country.

In that land, hemp was abundant and cheap, making it suitable for trade; after the two men finished their consultation, they paid money to purchase it, packed it according to the rules, loaded it onto a carrying pole, and set off, saying, "When we reach another state, we shall sell it as soon as there is profit."
They traveled on to another country and saw that *tūla* cotton was available at twice the profit; it could be made from hemp by converting the hemp into *tūla* cotton.
One man among them was wise and immediately traded his hemp for *tūla* cotton.
A certain person lacking wisdom said to his companion:
"I will not easily turn this hemp into tūla-cotton. Why is that?"
"Since I have used great effort to pack and tie this load of hemp and carry it from afar, I truly cannot exchange it.
That very day, the two men each carried their own goods and proceeded forward in succession until they reached another country.
In that country, the profit from silk was twice that of cotton; thus, a wise man there would trade his cotton for silk.
Another man, lacking wisdom, spoke as before:
"I cannot exchange my hemp for silk to seek further profit."
The two men took their goods and proceeded further until they reached a country where bolts of silk cloth were extremely cheap; compared to raw silk, the profit from them was twice as great.
A wise man among them, seeing that the profit was double, immediately exchanged his silk for the bolts of cloth.
The first, being ignorant, because he cherished his hemp, carried it from afar and refused to exchange it.

The two men, laden with their goods, continued forward until they reached a country that possessed only mines; there, fine silk was extremely expensive while silver was of very low value, so that by exchanging silk for silver, one would gain a hundredfold profit.
There was a wise man who sold silk to buy silver, expecting a hundredfold profit.
At that time, there was an unwise man who, because he thought this hemp had not yet reached a high price, cherished it and would not exchange it.
That one wise man further heard people say:
"In a certain country gold is produced, but silver is entirely absent.
He immediately called his companions and said they could go to that country.

Without passing much time, he arrived in that country. There, a wise man took his silver and exchanged it for gold. Having acquired the gold, he examined it with joy and thought to himself: "When I first left home, my wealth was extremely meager;

yet from the very beginning, when I bought the sesame seeds, I hoped for great profit. I never expected to reach this point and obtain gold—nothing in this world is more precious than this. Taking this back to my homeland, I shall surely attain great riches."
He immediately called his companions and said, "The years and months are passing; we may as well return to our country together.
Each provided for their honored parents according to what they had obtained.
Then the man carrying hemp said to his companion:

"I originally purchased this hemp hoping for a substantial profit, yet by the time we have reached this point, the profit has become quite meager. Since you now wish to turn back, how could I dare detain you?"
"Let us also carry these along as we return home, and wherever we encounter a high price, let us sell them.
Having concluded their deliberations, they chose an auspicious day and returned by the old road.

Not far from the capital, their kinsmen received news of their arrival; the family members all went out to the outskirts of the city to welcome them, filled with extraordinary joy, and each returned to their respective dwellings.
When the family that had obtained the gold was asked by their parents, wife, and children what profit they had gained, the head of the household replied:
"We have obtained gold with which we may become wealthy; we shall even be able to provide for our kinsmen."
The family members of that man carrying the hemp also asked him, "From now on, by managing this business, what profit will you obtain?
The man replied, "I shall obtain only this hemp; there will be no other goods."
Having heard this, the family members were deeply distressed in their hearts and said to that man:
"If you continue to manage affairs as you have done, our kinsmen will not escape poverty and lowliness."
"O Great King!
That man carrying hemp was by nature foolish and deluded; though he beheld the genuine gold, he refused to exchange it, thereby causing his kinsmen to suffer for a long time."
"It is just like a great king who, failing to recognize his own state, clings to the view of nihilism; for a long night he will suffer, and later regret will be difficult to overcome.
Upon hearing these words, the king addressed the Venerable One, saying:
"My mind does not turn back, for there is a reason.
It is because the people of this country are well-acquainted with my views; if I were to turn back from my convictions, the people would criticize me, saying:
'King Maṅgura always says that there is no self, no future world, and no rebirth by transformation.'"
"Today, on the contrary, I have been converted by Kāśyapa.
I certainly cannot endure such humiliation.
Kāśyapa replied:
"Great King!
I recall that in the past there was a man of undisciplined conduct who raised a herd of pigs for profit as his livelihood.

Once, he went elsewhere and seeing a great deal of filth and refuse, he gathered it up and loaded it on his back, intending to carry it home to feed his swine. Unexpectedly, he encountered torrential rain on the road; the filth soaked through his body and mind, and he immediately felt deep regret."
"Great King!
That person of immoral conduct was despised by the multitude because his body was defiled, yet he was still able to turn his mind back toward virtue.
You, however, occupy a position of supreme honor, yet you instead attend to frivolous words; you stubbornly cling to your own mind and do not abandon your nihilistic views."
At that time, Kāśyapa spoke again:
“Great King!
Previously, I employed various skillful metaphors in order to lead you, Great King, to abandon the view of nihilism, to know that there is a future life, and to have faith in the Triple Gem.”
"Great King, you have obstinately persisted in opposing me; now, for your sake once more, I shall provide another parable.
If you will believe it, listen attentively and receive it well, reflecting upon it with care."
The king said,
"Venerable One!
I pray that you will explain this to me."
At that time, Kāśyapa said to the Great King:
"I recall that in the past there was a pig named Mahodara.
Once, while Mahodara was leading a herd of pigs into the deep mountains and wilds, they suddenly encountered a lion within those mountains and forests."
Seeing the pig, the lion said to him, "I am the king of beasts; clear the way at once.
The pot-bellied one replied:
"If you wish for me to yield the path, it would be improper;
if you seek to challenge me to combat, I shall certainly not refuse.
Wait but a moment while I put on my armor."
Then the lion said:
"To what noble clan do you belong?
What is your name?"
"How dare you seek to challenge me to combat in such a manner?
As for the armor you require, it shall now be granted to you according to your wish.
Then that large-bellied one went to a pit of filth and smeared his entire body with it, returning to the lion and saying, "I am ready to fight you."
At that time, the lion replied to Mahodara:

"I am the king among all beasts; I constantly feed upon animals such as deer and gazelles. Even those who are inferior or weak I sometimes abandon and do not eat, let alone your impure and defiled body;
if I were to fight with you, it would truly defile me."
At that time, Siṃha immediately became Mahodara and spoke these verses:
"Your body was impure from the start; now it is further added to by stench and filth.
If you intend to seek a fight, I shall fall upon you."
Venerable Kāśyapa replied to the Great King:
"What Your Majesty has seen is like that of a pig fighting a lion; I am like the lion who has already fallen upon you."
When King Prajāpatirāja heard these words spoken by the Venerable Kāśyapa, he felt deep remorse from the bottom of his heart and said to Kāśyapa:
"Venerable One!

From the moment I first heard the parable of the sun and moon, I had already believed and submitted. However, wishing to hear of the Venerable’s wisdom and eloquence, I used those words to provoke and draw forth this teaching."
"I only pray, Venerable One!
Examine my sincere heart and recognize my faithful submission; I vow to take refuge in the Venerable Kāśyapa.
Kāśyapa replied:
"Do not take refuge in me; my refuge is the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. You should likewise take refuge in them. The King replied again:

"In accordance with the Venerable One’s instruction, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and receive the lay precepts (*upāsaka-śīla*). From this day forward, I vow not to kill, not to steal, not to engage in sexual misconduct, not to lie, and furthermore, not to drink alcohol; for as long as life lasts, I shall uphold the pure precepts of the Buddha."

At that time, having received the transformative guidance, the Great King turned his sincere heart toward the Buddha and accepted the Three Refuges; he vowed to uphold the Five Precepts forever and, together with the brahmins and elders, withdrew after prostrating with great joy and exultation.
The Great Chapter on the King of Phrases, Scroll Lower
